title: Tara and the Sun's Secret
markdown:
Nestled beside Bright Meadow, which buzzed each year with rustling leaves and sweet earth, lived Tara, whose mind was as keen as a freshly sharpened pencil and whose heart was as warm as a sunbeam after rain. She loved numbers, patterns, and the quiet thrill of mysteries. The world was a magnificent puzzle.

This year she had a plan as carefully drawn as a star chart. She had measured and mapped her garden, decided where each seed should nestle, and drawn the most efficient watering schedule down to the last dewdrop. Helping her: Sprig, a frog whose croaks were tiny bells, and wise Dr Kellan, a retired botanist whose white beard often tangled with stray leaves. Forest folk whispered he knew more about plants than anyone in Bright Meadow.

“My Super-Sunflower will be the tallest,” Tara declared, tapping a perfect diagram. “And my Rainbow Roses will make a real rainbow blush.”

Days unfurled. A puzzle arrived. The Super-Sunflower was no taller than her boot. The Rainbow Roses, instead of fiery reds and sunny yellows, were a shy pale pink. Sprig blinked golden eyes. “Ribbit. Not quite spectacular.”

Kellan, tending a wilting buttercup, sighed, beard rustling. “Your calculations are usually as perfect as a spider’s silk.”

Tara paced the gravel, boots crunching. Mrs Gable’s pumpkins were practically rolling onto the path. Young Timmy’s beans climbed like determined mountaineers. “My numbers were right. I checked them twice.”

One afternoon, as the sun began its slow descent, orange and pink and lavender, Tara sat by the struggling sunflowers. Sprig hopped onto a flat stone and looked at the sky.

“The sun,” Tara murmured. “It’s moving, as always. But it feels different. When I planted, it seemed high and strong, overhead. Now it feels lower. The light comes from the side.”

Kellan chuckled, eyes twinkling. “You’ve noticed. It doesn’t always sit directly overhead. Its path and angle change. Trees remember: they reach. This old oak leans a little south, always after the sun it gets. Light changes its path and its strength with the time of year. A grand slow dance.”

Tara understood. The numbers were not wrong. She had forgotten time. The sun’s angle — the light and warmth her plants received — changed through the months. Her Super-Sunflower, planted for maximum summer sun, was getting less of it now that autumn was arriving. The plants needed to adapt. So did her plan.

They sprang to work. Plants that needed more direct light were dug and set where the afternoon sun was still strong. Others that preferred a gentler touch went into soft shade. Sprig’s strong little legs nudged pebbles to guide water. Tara calculated new angles and positions, brow furrowed with excitement. Pale roses blushed. Sunflowers straightened their necks.

When the Bright Meadow Garden Competition arrived, Tara’s garden was not a riot of towering giants. It was a tapestry that shifted with the changing light, in step with the year. The judges, who had always looked for biggest and brightest, murmured as they walked.

“It’s different.”

“It’s truly beautiful.”

Tara stepped forward, quiet pride. “We understood the sun. Earth is tilted. As it travels around the sun, the light we get here changes. That’s seasons. This garden is planned not just for now, but for the sun’s journey.”

She did not need old Hoot to finish it. The oak’s lean said enough. That night the moon climbed, silver on the blooms, and Tara noted the new angles in her book, and wondered what else might be waiting in a number she had not yet thought to include — a tilt, a month, a leaning tree. Sprig croaked once, spectacular enough, and the buttercup Dr Kellan had tended looked less like a sigh.
characters: Tara (a maths detective), Sprig (a frog), Kellan (a botanist)
